case_analysis.focal_point: Whether courts reviewing an agency’s interpretation of an ambiguous statute must defer to the agency under Chevron, or instead independently determine the statute’s best meaning under the Administrative Procedure Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706 (especially § 706(2)(A) and the directive that courts “decide all relevant questions of law”); Magnuson–Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (16 U.S.C. §§ 1801 et seq.) as the underlying regulatory statute being interpreted by the National Marine Fisheries Service.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (fishing businesses) argue that the agency lacked statutory authority to require industry-funded at-sea monitors and that the D.C. Circuit upheld the rule only by applying Chevron deference; they contend Chevron is inconsistent with the APA’s command that courts independently decide questions of law, enables agencies to expand their own power absent clear congressional authorization, and should be overruled or at least sharply limited so courts apply ordinary interpretive tools to determine the best reading of the statute.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Commerce/NMFS) argue that Chevron is a settled, workable framework reflecting congressional delegation and institutional competence—agencies, not courts, are better positioned to make policy-laden choices within statutory ambiguity; they maintain the agency’s interpretation is reasonable (and thus lawful under Chevron) and emphasize reliance interests and stability in administrative law that would be disrupted if Chevron were overruled.
key_precedents: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984)
National Cable & Telecommunications Assn. v. Brand X Internet Services (2005)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point—that Chevron can be defended as a background rule of construction consistent with Skidmore-era practice—still does not answer the APA’s textual allocation in § 706 that courts “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutory provisions, a duty that is difficult to square with Chevron’s mandatory acceptance of any “reasonable” agency view after ambiguity is found. Justice Sotomayor is right to stress reliance and administrability, and Mead and Kisor confirm the need for disciplined, tool-exhausting review; but those precedents cut against automatic deference by requiring courts to do the interpretive work first, which makes Chevron’s step-two tie-breaker look less like interpretation and more like a transfer of interpretive primacy. A narrower, legitimacy-preserving path is to reaffirm independent judicial judgment as the default under § 706 while preserving Skidmore’s persuasive respect for expert agency reasoning, thereby minimizing disruption without perpetuating a regime that displaces the judiciary’s role. Applying that approach here, the Magnuson–Stevens Act lacks clear authorization for an industry-funded monitor mandate, so the agency action exceeds statutory authority under § 706(2)(C).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Chevron is merely a permissible “rule of statutory construction” consistent with historical Skidmore-style respect for agency views, but that collapses the key distinction: Skidmore allows persuasion, whereas Chevron compels acceptance of an agency’s view even when the court believes another reading is best. The APA’s text—especially § 706’s command that courts “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret … statutory provisions,” coupled with § 706(2)(C)’s duty to set aside action “in excess of statutory … authority”—requires independent judicial judgment, not a default transfer of interpretive primacy to the Executive. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance-interest and expertise arguments cannot override that enacted text and the Constitution’s separation of powers; if Congress wishes to authorize industry-funded monitors or delegate such policy choices, it must do so clearly in the statute. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that, at most, the agency may receive Skidmore’s persuasive weight, but Chevron’s mandatory deference is inconsistent with § 706 and should not control this case.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point—that Chevron is just a historical “rule of construction” akin to Skidmore—does not answer the APA’s textual assignment of interpretive responsibility to courts: § 706 says we “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret … statutory provisions,” which is incompatible with a mandatory tie-breaker that compels acceptance of any “reasonable” agency view. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 706(2)(C)’s command to set aside action “in excess of statutory … authority” presupposes independent judicial judgment about statutory limits; Chevron’s step two dilutes that duty by treating ambiguity as a delegation. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance and administrability concerns are serious, but they cannot override enacted text, and Mead/Kisor—rather than validating Chevron—underscore that we have already required courts to exhaust interpretive tools and thus moved toward a best-reading approach with, at most, Skidmore-style persuasive weight. On that understanding, the agency’s attempt to impose industry-funded monitors requires clear statutory authorization; absent it, the action exceeds statutory authority.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s textual point about § 706—courts “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutes—is the most serious challenge, but it does not follow that calibrated deference is forbidden; courts can still “decide” the law while recognizing that, in certain administrable, technical schemes, Congress has effectively assigned policy-laden gap-filling to expert agencies as part of the interpretive enterprise. Justice Barrett’s reliance on § 706(2)(C) (“in excess of statutory … authority”) assumes that any ambiguity-triggered deference necessarily cedes the boundary-setting function, yet Mead and Kisor already require courts to exhaust traditional tools and police the limits of delegation before any controlling weight attaches—cabining Chevron rather than making it irreconcilable with the APA. Justice Jackson’s preference for Skidmore-only review underestimates how often persuasiveness review invites ad hoc judicial policy choice in complex regulatory regimes, increasing instability and undermining protections that vulnerable communities rely on. On this statute and record, I would apply Chevron as narrowed by Mead/Kisor and uphold NMFS’s reasonable interpretation rather than adopt an across-the-board Skidmore regime that effectively overrules Chevron without clearer congressional instruction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: § 706 says courts “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutes, which they read to forbid any rule that ever gives binding weight to agency interpretations. But that reading quietly assumes that “decide” and “interpret” in 1946 necessarily meant a single best-reading, non-deferential model, whereas contemporaneous practice (as reflected in Skidmore) treated an agency’s considered, expert, and consistent view as a legitimate interpretive input that a court could weigh while still deciding the legal question. Mead and Kisor strengthen the case for tightening Chevron—requiring genuine ambiguity after exhausting the traditional tools and looking for indicia that Congress meant the agency to fill administrable gaps—but they do not compel the Chief’s proposed across-the-board replacement of Chevron with “best reading + Skidmore” as a matter of APA text. Given the APA’s lack of a clear anti-deference command and the disruption to statutory coherence and reliance interests that Justice Sotomayor highlights, I do not think § 706 justifies overruling Chevron wholesale to resolve this case.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s effort to recast Chevron as a mere “rule of construction” grounded in Skidmore-era practice does not answer the APA’s enacted instruction that courts “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret … statutory provisions,” which most naturally demands independent judicial judgment rather than mandatory acceptance of an agency’s view whenever ambiguity remains. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 706(2)(C)’s duty to set aside action “in excess of statutory … authority” presupposes the court itself determines statutory limits, a task Chevron step two dilutes by making “reasonableness” the endpoint instead of best meaning. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance and administrability concerns are serious, but under a textualist approach they cannot rewrite § 706’s allocation of interpretive responsibility; Skidmore’s persuasive-weight framework can accommodate expertise without transferring interpretive primacy. Mead and Kisor, rather than saving Chevron, confirm our trajectory toward requiring courts to exhaust traditional interpretive tools and then still decide the statute’s meaning—making Chevron’s binding tie-breaker increasingly irreconcilable with the judicial role the APA codifies.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point—that Chevron can be treated as a background rule of construction consistent with Skidmore-era practice and protected by reliance interests—does not, for me, overcome the APA’s enacted text. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, § 706 directs that courts “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutes, and § 706(2)(C) requires setting aside agency action “in excess of statutory … authority”; that structure is difficult to reconcile with a mandatory tie-breaker that makes the agency’s reasonable view controlling once ambiguity is declared. Mead and Kisor (raised by Roberts and Barrett) reinforce that our doctrine has already moved toward courts exhausting traditional tools and treating agency views as persuasive rather than controlling, which makes a Skidmore-respect framework a narrower, more institutionally stable way to account for expertise without ceding interpretive primacy. I therefore remain with petitioners: absent clear statutory authorization in the Magnuson–Stevens Act for the industry-funded monitor requirement, the agency has exceeded its authority under § 706(2)(C).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is that Chevron can be characterized as a background “rule of construction” consistent with Skidmore-era respect for agency expertise, but that framing does not fit § 706’s text assigning courts the duty to “decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutes—tasks that presuppose independent judgment rather than mandatory acceptance of any reasonable agency view once ambiguity is found. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, § 706(2)(C)’s instruction to set aside action “in excess of statutory … authority” reinforces that the court must itself determine statutory limits, which Chevron step two blurs by relocating interpretive primacy to the agency. Mead and Kisor, cited by Justice Sotomayor and others, affect the analysis by confirming our precedent has already insisted on exhausting traditional tools and limiting automatic deference—developments that undermine the claim that Chevron is an APA-consistent default rather than confirm it. Reliance and administrability concerns, though substantial (Justice Sotomayor), are better handled through stare decisis-sensitive application and Skidmore’s persuasive-weight framework than by retaining a doctrine that conflicts with the APA’s best reading.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point—that Chevron can be recast as a historically grounded rule of statutory construction akin to Skidmore and therefore compatible with § 706—does not, for me, overcome the qualitative shift Chevron introduces: mandatory acceptance of an agency’s “reasonable” view even when the court concludes another reading is best. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s emphasis on § 706’s directive that courts “shall decide” questions of law and police actions “in excess of statutory … authority” fits better with a model of independent judicial judgment plus persuasive respect, rather than ambiguity-triggered interpretive primacy for the agency. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance and administrability concerns are serious, but as Justice Kavanaugh notes, those concerns can be addressed through a Skidmore framework and ordinary stare decisis/retroactivity tools without preserving a deference rule that weakens meaningful judicial review—particularly where the agency interpretation expands coercive power over regulated parties. Mead and Kisor, which Justice Sotomayor invokes to cabin Chevron, ultimately reinforce my view that we already require courts to exhaust interpretive tools and thus should acknowledge forthrightly that § 706 calls for courts to decide statutory meaning, considering agency expertise as persuasion rather than command.

John Roberts.reasoning: The APA directs that a reviewing court “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret constitutional and statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, and it further requires courts to set aside agency action “in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitations,” § 706(2)(C); that text is difficult to square with a mandatory rule of deference on pure questions of statutory meaning. Our post-Chevron decisions have already narrowed the circumstances in which deference is warranted—Mead requires congressional authorization and an exercise of lawmaking power, and Kisor stresses that courts must exhaust the traditional tools of interpretation before yielding—confirming that Chevron cannot be an across-the-board command. Given the substantial reliance interests in administrative law, the proper course is to resolve this case on narrow grounds by holding that courts must independently determine the statute’s best reading under § 706 and may consider an agency’s views only for their persuasive force (Skidmore), rather than reflexively deferring whenever a statute is ambiguous. On that understanding, the rule compelling industry-funded monitors requires clear statutory authorization in the Magnuson–Stevens Act, and absent it the agency has acted beyond its authority under § 706(2)(C).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Administrative Procedure Act requires that “the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret constitutional and statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which directs courts to exercise independent judgment rather than defer to an agency’s preferred reading of an ambiguous statute. Chevron deference is therefore inconsistent with the APA’s text and improperly transfers the judicial power to “say what the law is” from Article III courts to executive agencies, enabling agencies to expand their own authority absent clear congressional authorization. Consistent with my longstanding view that statutory meaning is a question of law for courts to decide and that courts never defer on legal questions (see my dissent respecting denial of certiorari in Baldwin v. United States), the Court should reject Chevron and determine the best reading of the Magnuson–Stevens Act itself. At most, an agency’s view may receive Skidmore’s limited persuasive weight, but it cannot control the meaning of the statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The APA’s text directs that a “reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret constitutional and statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which is difficult to reconcile with Chevron’s mandatory rule requiring courts to accept any “reasonable” agency reading of an ambiguous statute rather than determining the statute’s best meaning. Section 706(2) further requires courts to set aside agency action “in excess of statutory jurisdiction [or] authority,” § 706(2)(C), a task that presupposes independent judicial judgment about statutory limits. While Skidmore allows courts to give an agency’s reasoning persuasive weight, it does not transfer the interpretive duty to the agency, and Mead’s emphasis on when Congress has truly delegated interpretive authority underscores that broad, automatic Chevron deference exceeds what the APA contemplates. Given the practical risk that Chevron invites agencies to expand their own power absent clear congressional authorization, I would side with petitioners and require courts to exercise independent judgment under § 706.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 706 of the APA directs courts to “decide all relevant questions of law,” but our post-APA cases have reconciled that duty with calibrated deference where Congress has implicitly or explicitly left policy-laden gaps for agencies to fill, as reflected in Chevron’s two-step framework. Mead and Skidmore confirm that deference is not automatic and depends on indicia of delegated authority and the agency’s reasoned decisionmaking, but where those conditions are met, courts may respect agency expertise without abdicating judicial review under § 706(2)(A)’s “arbitrary [or] capricious” constraint. Given the reliance interests and administrability concerns recognized in our modern administrative-law cases, overruling Chevron wholesale would destabilize settled regulatory regimes that protect workers, consumers, and other vulnerable communities, while shifting policymaking to courts less equipped to weigh technical tradeoffs. Applying Chevron as limited by Mead’s delegation inquiry, I would uphold deference to NMFS’s reasonable interpretation of the Magnuson–Stevens Act in this context.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The APA’s instruction that reviewing courts “decide all relevant questions of law” in § 706 does not compel abandonment of Chevron, because at the time of the APA’s enactment courts continued to give weight to agency interpretations of law, as reflected in Skidmore’s respect-based approach and early post-APA decisions that did not read § 706 to forbid deference. Properly understood, Chevron operates as a rule of statutory construction: where Congress has left an ambiguity in a statute an agency administers, courts still use ordinary interpretive tools at step one, and only if genuine ambiguity remains do they accept a reasonable agency choice at step two. That framework is workable and promotes statutory coherence in complex regulatory schemes like the Magnuson–Stevens Act, consistent with Mead’s limits on when deference applies and Kisor’s emphasis on cabining deference doctrines rather than discarding them wholesale. Overruling Chevron based on § 706 would disrupt settled reliance interests without a clear textual command in the APA to do so.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Administrative Procedure Act directs that a reviewing court “shall decide all relevant questions of law,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, and further requires setting aside agency action “not in accordance with law” or “in excess of statutory jurisdiction [or] authority,” § 706(2)(A), (C)—text that calls for independent judicial judgment about statutory meaning rather than compulsory deference whenever a statute is deemed “ambiguous.” Chevron’s regime effectively transfers to the Executive the Judiciary’s duty to say what the law is, unsettling separation of powers and allowing agencies to expand their own power without clear congressional authorization. Whatever persuasive weight an agency view may merit under Skidmore, courts should determine the statute’s best meaning using ordinary interpretive tools, not default to an agency’s “reasonable” construction. Because the D.C. Circuit upheld the industry-funded monitor requirement only by applying Chevron, the judgment should be reversed and the statute interpreted independently under § 706.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The APA directs that a reviewing court “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret … statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which is difficult to square with a mandatory rule requiring courts to defer to an agency’s view of statutory meaning whenever the court finds ambiguity. Our post-Chevron decisions have already narrowed deference through prerequisites tied to statutory text and context (Mead) and by recognizing that agency interpretations at most warrant persuasive weight depending on their reasoning and consistency (Skidmore). Given the Court’s duty under § 706(2)(A) and § 706(2)(C) to set aside agency action “not in accordance with law” or “in excess of statutory … authority,” and considering practical concerns about agencies expanding their own power absent clear congressional authorization, I would independently determine the statute’s best meaning rather than apply Chevron as a controlling command. That approach preserves stability by retaining Skidmore-style respect where warranted while restoring the judiciary’s assigned role in statutory interpretation and avoiding the legitimacy costs and workability problems that Chevron has produced.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The APA’s text directs that “the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret … statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which is most naturally read to require independent judicial judgment about statutory meaning rather than mandatory deference whenever a statute is ambiguous. While Chevron (1984) adopted a two-step framework that can treat ambiguity as an implicit delegation to the agency, that approach sits uneasily with § 706’s command and with this Court’s later efforts to confine deference doctrines to their justifications and limits, see Mead (limiting Chevron to certain agency actions) and Kisor (cabining deference even in the interpretive domain). At minimum, courts should determine the statute’s best meaning using ordinary interpretive tools, and any persuasive weight given to an agency’s view should resemble Skidmore’s respect based on reasoning and consistency rather than Chevron’s binding deference. Given that the D.C. Circuit upheld the rule by relying on Chevron rather than a best-reading analysis under § 706, petitioners have the better view of the APA’s instruction and the judicial role.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The APA directs reviewing courts to “decide all relevant questions of law,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, and to set aside agency action “not in accordance with law,” § 706(2)(A), which is best read to require independent judicial judgment about statutory meaning rather than mandatory deference whenever a court finds ambiguity. Consistent with United States v. Mead Corp., Chevron should at minimum be limited to circumstances where Congress clearly delegated interpretive authority with the force of law, and absent that clear delegation the agency’s view should receive only Skidmore’s respect proportional to its persuasiveness. A persuasiveness-based approach preserves procedural fairness and meaningful judicial review while still crediting agency expertise and practical consequences, and it avoids allowing agencies to expand their own power without clear congressional authorization. Accordingly, courts should not treat ambiguity alone as a trigger for controlling deference, but should determine the statute’s best meaning under ordinary tools of interpretation, using Skidmore factors as appropriate.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether courts should continue to apply Chevron deference—deferring to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute—or instead independently interpret statutes under the Administrative Procedure Act when reviewing agency action.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706 (especially § 706(2)(A) and the direction that courts 'decide all relevant questions of law'); underlying regulatory statute: Magnuson–Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, 16 U.S.C. § 1801 et seq. (as applied to the National Marine Fisheries Service’s authority to require industry-funded at-sea monitors).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (fishing companies) argue that the agency lacked statutory authority to require them to pay for federal observers/monitors and that the D.C. Circuit upheld the rule only by relying on Chevron’s framework; they contend Chevron is inconsistent with the APA and separation-of-powers principles because it transfers to agencies the judiciary’s duty to say what the law is, and they urge the Court to overrule or substantially narrow Chevron so that courts exercise independent judgment on statutory meaning rather than deferring to an agency whenever ambiguity exists and the agency’s view is 'reasonable.'
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Department of Commerce/NMFS) argue that Chevron is a longstanding, workable rule of decision reflecting congressional choice to delegate interpretive discretion to expert agencies when statutes are ambiguous; they maintain that stability and reliance interests counsel strongly against overruling Chevron, and that in areas involving technical regulatory programs (like fisheries management) agencies are institutionally better situated than courts to make policy-laden choices within statutory bounds—so courts should continue to uphold reasonable agency interpretations where Congress has left gaps.
key_precedents: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984)
National Cable & Telecommunications Ass'n v. Brand X Internet Services (2005)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson offer the strongest reconciliation: under Mead’s force-of-law trigger, a court can “decide” that Congress delegated gap-filling discretion and thus apply a reasonableness standard without surrendering the judicial role. But under my minimalist, text-first approach, that harmonization still gives residual ambiguity a dispositive, transferrable effect that is difficult to square with § 706’s command that the reviewing court “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutory provisions—especially once Kisor’s insistence on exhausting traditional tools is taken seriously, which points toward independent judgment with persuasive respect (Skidmore), not mandatory acceptance. Mead is relevant, but it narrows when deference might arise; it does not answer the antecedent APA question of who ultimately interprets the statute once the court has done the ordinary work of construction. On the merits, even without announcing any broader rule than necessary, the Magnuson–Stevens Act does not clearly authorize compelled industry funding for monitors, so the rule is “in excess of statutory…authority” under § 706(2)(C) and cannot be sustained merely by invoking deference.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor argue that § 706 can be “harmonized” with Chevron on a theory of implicit delegation in regulatory gaps, but that approach inverts the APA’s textual command that courts “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret…statutory provisions.” Mead’s force-of-law prerequisite, which Justice Kagan invokes, narrows Chevron but does not cure the core problem: even within Mead’s domain, Chevron still requires a court to accept an agency’s reasonable construction rather than exercise independent judgment about statutory meaning, contrary to § 706 and Article III’s allocation of the judicial power. Skidmore supplies the historically grounded alternative—respect proportional to persuasiveness—without transferring the judicial duty of interpretation to the Executive. Because the D.C. Circuit sustained the monitor-funding requirement only through Chevron rather than independent interpretation of the Magnuson–Stevens Act under § 706(2)(A) and (C), the judgment should be reversed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s harmonization theory—that a court can “decide” under § 706 by finding a Mead-qualifying delegation and then applying a reasonableness standard—remains the most substantial defense of Chevron, but it still treats residual ambiguity as a transfer of interpretive primacy that § 706’s text does not supply. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 706’s command that courts “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret…statutory provisions” is most naturally read to require the court’s independent best judgment on meaning, with agency views receiving only Skidmore weight when persuasive, not controlling force at step two. Mead and Kisor, which Justice Sotomayor invokes as disciplining devices, narrow when deference might apply, but they do not cure the core mismatch: even after exhausting interpretive tools, Chevron obliges acceptance of a merely “reasonable” agency view instead of the court’s own interpretation. And on the merits, compelling regulated parties to fund federal monitors without clear statutory authorization is exactly the sort of consequential assertion of power that § 706(2)(C) should invalidate rather than sustain through deference.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 706’s command that courts “shall decide” questions of law sounds like independent judgment—has force, but it does not foreclose a framework in which the court first decides, using all traditional tools (as Kisor demands), whether Congress has delegated policy-laden gap-filling authority to an agency acting with the force of law (as Mead describes). In that circumstance, applying a reasonableness standard is not “yielding interpretive primacy” so much as enforcing the statute’s own legal criterion for permissible implementation, while still policing statutory limits under § 706(2)(C) and arbitrariness under § 706(2)(A). Justice Gorsuch’s concern that ambiguity lets agencies “enlarge their own power” is mitigated by a rigorous step-one inquiry and by refusing deference where an agency claims new coercive authority of major consequence absent clear statutory footing—without adopting a categorical, APA-text-based overruling that would unsettle protective regulatory regimes in ways that matter for real people. Because the opposing side has not shown that § 706 unmistakably compels Skidmore-only review in all residual-ambiguity cases, I remain with Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson on harmonization rather than abandonment.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is textual: § 706 says courts “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutes, which resists any automatic, ambiguity-triggered transfer of interpretive primacy to agencies. But I do not read Chevron (properly cabined by Mead and Kisor) as relieving courts of that duty; the court first uses the traditional tools to decide whether Congress has made “reasonableness within delegated bounds” the operative legal standard, and then enforces those bounds under § 706(2)(C)—that is still the court deciding the question of law. Justice Thomas’s Skidmore-only alternative avoids the “mandatory acceptance” label, but it risks smuggling in ad hoc judicial policymaking in technical regimes where Congress plausibly chose an administrable, reasonableness-based standard via force-of-law procedures (Mead). On the Magnuson–Stevens merits, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Alito’s “clear authorization” framing because the statute’s structure can support the monitoring program without treating the cost feature as categorically ultra vires absent a direct textual conflict.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that § 706 can be “harmonized” with Chevron because Congress sometimes delegates gap-filling discretion to expert agencies, especially under technical statutes like Magnuson–Stevens. But § 706’s text assigns to “the reviewing court” the duty to “decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutes; treating ambiguity itself as a transfer of interpretive power reverses that ordinary allocation and lets agencies enlarge their own authority by finding uncertainty. Mead’s force-of-law limits do not solve the basic problem, because even where notice-and-comment rules are involved, the question remains who decides the statute’s meaning—and the APA answers: courts, giving agency views only such weight as their reasoning warrants under Skidmore. Reliance interests and administrability concerns, which Justice Jackson emphasizes, are not a license to persist in a doctrine that sits uneasily with the statutory command and separation-of-powers first principles, particularly where the agency asserts power to impose significant private financial obligations absent clear statutory authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s Mead-based harmonization is the strongest defense of Chevron, but it still treats residual ambiguity as a legal switch that transfers interpretive primacy to the agency, which is hard to reconcile with § 706’s command that the reviewing court “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutory provisions. As the Chief Justice notes, Kisor and Mead have pushed us toward more rigorous judicial work before any deference applies, and that trajectory fits better with independent judgment plus Skidmore persuasiveness than with a mandatory acceptance rule at step two. Justice Jackson’s reliance-interest point is important institutionally, but under my methodology it cannot override the APA’s textual allocation of interpretive responsibility to courts, especially where (as Justice Alito emphasizes) the agency claims authority to impose significant private financial obligations without clear statutory authorization. I therefore stay with Petitioner: § 706 requires courts to decide the best meaning of the Magnuson–Stevens Act, considering the agency’s view for whatever persuasive value it has, and the rule fails under that review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s harmonization theory—treating residual ambiguity in a Mead-qualified, force-of-law setting as an implicit delegation that makes “reasonableness” the operative legal standard—most directly confronts the APA text, but it still does not square with § 706’s instruction that the reviewing court “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutory provisions. Under a textualist, original-public-meaning approach, those verbs assign the interpretive judgment to courts; a court cannot satisfy that duty by declaring ambiguity and then treating the agency’s view as controlling, rather than merely persuasive in the Skidmore sense. Kisor’s insistence on exhausting traditional tools before any deference reinforces that the judiciary’s job is to reach the best reading of the statute, not to stop at a threshold finding and yield interpretive primacy. Even putting the APA issue aside, I remain unconvinced the Magnuson–Stevens Act clearly authorizes compelling regulated parties to fund federal monitors, so the rule is invalid under § 706(2)(C) absent a deference regime that the APA’s text does not support.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest point: § 706’s command that courts “shall decide” questions of law and “interpret” statutes sounds like independent judicial judgment, not a mandatory rule of acceptance. But I remain persuaded by Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s reconciliation: the court still “decides” by using traditional tools to determine whether Congress, in a force-of-law scheme (Mead), has made reasonableness within delegated bounds the governing legal standard, while continuing to invalidate actions “in excess of statutory…authority” under § 706(2)(C) and arbitrary actions under § 706(2)(A). Justice Thomas’s Skidmore-only approach has textual appeal, yet under my pragmatic, consequences-sensitive methodology it undervalues Congress’s practical use of expert, procedurally constrained policymaking and risks destabilizing reliance interests without a clearer indication that § 706 was meant to silently repeal that delegation framework. On this record, I do not see the APA-text argument as sufficiently undermining the narrowed Chevron/Mead structure to warrant switching sides, even as I agree we should emphasize a rigorous step-one and robust (C) policing to address the “agency enlarges its power” concern Justice Gorsuch raises.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Administrative Procedure Act directs that the “reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret…statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which sits uneasily with Chevron’s presumption that ambiguity triggers deference rather than independent judicial judgment. Our post-Chevron decisions have already narrowed deference through threshold limits on when it applies, see United States v. Mead Corp. (requiring indications of congressionally delegated lawmaking authority) and the emphasis on rigorous judicial inquiry before yielding interpretive control, consistent with Kisor v. Wilkie’s retrenchment in a closely related deference context. To preserve institutional legitimacy and reliance interests, the better course is not to extend Chevron further, but to resolve this case on the APA’s command that courts independently determine statutory meaning and then assess whether the agency acted “in excess of statutory…authority” or “not in accordance with law,” § 706(2)(A), (C). Under that approach, the agency must identify clear statutory authorization in the Magnuson–Stevens Act to impose industry-funded monitoring obligations, and absent it the rule cannot stand.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Administrative Procedure Act directs that a reviewing court “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret ... statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which reflects the traditional understanding at the time of enactment that statutory interpretation is a judicial duty, not one to be transferred to the Executive. Chevron’s rule of mandatory deference to an agency’s “reasonable” view of ambiguity conflicts with that text and with the separation-of-powers principle that it is “emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” At most, agency views may receive persuasive weight under Skidmore v. Swift & Co. (1944), but courts must exercise independent judgment on statutory meaning under § 706 when reviewing agency action under § 706(2)(A). Because the D.C. Circuit upheld the industry-funded monitor requirement only by resort to Chevron rather than independent statutory interpretation under the Magnuson–Stevens Act, the judgment should be reversed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The APA instructs that a reviewing court “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret constitutional and statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, language that is difficult to reconcile with a regime in which courts surrender interpretive judgment whenever a statute is deemed “ambiguous” and the agency’s view is merely “reasonable.” While this Court has already curtailed deference doctrines in cases like Kisor v. Wilkie (tightening Auer) and limited Chevron’s domain through United States v. Mead Corp., Chevron’s broad presumption of delegation is not grounded in § 706’s text and has produced serious practical consequences by shifting lawmaking power to executive agencies. In a case involving the imposition of significant compliance costs—requiring private parties to fund monitors under the Magnuson–Stevens Act—courts should independently determine whether Congress actually authorized that result, rather than treating statutory silence or uncertainty as a license for agency policymaking. Accordingly, the proper course is to reject Chevron-style deference and require independent judicial interpretation under the APA’s command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I would decline to overrule Chevron and continue to afford deference to reasonable agency interpretations where Congress has left genuine ambiguity, consistent with Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. NRDC (1984) and the Court’s later tailoring in United States v. Mead Corp. (2001). The APA’s instruction that courts “decide all relevant questions of law,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, can be harmonized with Chevron by understanding that Congress may delegate interpretive discretion to expert agencies in administering complex statutory schemes like the Magnuson–Stevens Act, so long as courts police statutory limits and set aside actions “in excess of statutory jurisdiction,” § 706(2)(C). Replacing Chevron with purely independent judicial interpretation risks destabilizing settled regulatory programs and undermining workable, expert-driven administration in technical areas, while offering little additional protection to vulnerable communities that depend on effective environmental and fisheries enforcement. At minimum, any recalibration should track Mead/Skidmore’s attention to procedural formality and persuasiveness rather than a wholesale repudiation that invites courts to substitute their policy judgments for agencies’ within statutory bounds.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The APA’s instruction that courts “decide all relevant questions of law,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, does not foreclose giving interpretive weight to agencies when Congress has conferred gap-filling authority; it is compatible with Chevron’s allocation of interpretive responsibility within statutory bounds. Under United States v. Mead Corp., Chevron deference applies when Congress delegated authority to act with the force of law and the agency interpretation was issued in exercise of that authority—conditions typically satisfied by notice-and-comment fisheries regulations under the Magnuson–Stevens Act. Given the Act’s broad management framework and the practical need for workable, expert administration in technical programs, a reasonable agency reading to implement observer requirements—including associated compliance mechanisms—falls within the kind of delegated discretion Chevron and Mead contemplate. Overruling Chevron wholesale would unsettle reliance interests and destabilize administrative law, while existing limits (Mead’s force-of-law requirement and Skidmore’s persuasiveness review when Chevron does not apply) already prevent reflexive deference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Administrative Procedure Act instructs that “the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret ... statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, a textual command that sits uneasily with Chevron’s rule requiring judges to yield to an agency’s “reasonable” reading whenever a court perceives ambiguity. Respect for separation of powers reinforces that point: Article III courts must exercise independent judgment about what the law is, and agencies may not expand their own authority by converting statutory silence into delegated power, especially where the agency claims power to impose substantial financial burdens. Our pre-Chevron tradition reflected in Skidmore permitted respect proportional to an agency’s persuasiveness, not binding deference that displaces judicial interpretation, and Kisor’s narrowing of Auer underscores that reflexive deference is in tension with the judiciary’s duty to say what the law is. Accordingly, courts should interpret the Magnuson–Stevens Act independently under § 706 and set aside agency action “in excess of statutory jurisdiction [or] authority,” § 706(2)(C), rather than uphold it through Chevron’s framework.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The APA instructs that “the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “determine the meaning or applicability of the terms of an agency action,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which is most naturally read to require independent judicial judgment on statutory meaning rather than automatic deference whenever ambiguity exists. Chevron’s broad deference regime has proven increasingly unworkable in practice and has created instability and unfair surprise, as reflected by the Court’s subsequent narrowing moves in cases such as Mead and by the Court’s insistence in Kisor that deference doctrines must be tightly cabined and grounded in traditional interpretive tools. Consistent with history, tradition, and separation of powers, courts can give agencies appropriate weight under Skidmore based on persuasiveness and expertise, but the judiciary must ultimately say what the law is when reviewing whether agency action is “in accordance with law” or “in excess of statutory authority” under § 706(2)(A) and (C). Therefore, I would not continue to apply Chevron as a controlling rule of decision and would vote for the fishing companies.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The APA’s text directs that a reviewing court “shall decide all relevant questions of law” and “interpret…statutory provisions,” 5 U.S.C. § 706, which in ordinary legal usage assigns independent judgment about statutory meaning to courts rather than requiring deference whenever ambiguity is found. Whatever room Congress may leave for agencies to exercise policymaking discretion within statutory bounds, that discretion must be grounded in the statute as best read by the court; Chevron’s two-step framework too readily treats ambiguity as an implicit delegation of interpretive authority in tension with § 706’s command and with separation-of-powers concerns. Precedents like Mead and Skidmore show that agency views can earn respect proportional to their persuasiveness and procedural pedigree without displacing the judiciary’s duty to say what the law is. Applying independent interpretation here, the Magnuson–Stevens Act’s structure and specific funding provisions do not clearly authorize compelling industry to pay for federal monitors, so the rule cannot be sustained on deference alone.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The APA’s instruction that reviewing courts “decide all relevant questions of law” in 5 U.S.C. § 706 does not, standing alone, compel overruling Chevron; rather, this Court has long harmonized § 706 with deference where Congress has left interpretive discretion to agencies administering complex regulatory programs. Under United States v. Mead Corp. (2001), Chevron applies only when Congress has delegated authority to make rules with the force of law and the agency interpretation was promulgated through that delegated lawmaking; otherwise, the agency receives only Skidmore respect, which preserves meaningful judicial oversight and procedural fairness. Given reliance interests and the Court’s incremental approach to deference reflected in Mead and Kisor v. Wilkie (2019), the better course is to retain Chevron’s narrowed, cabined framework rather than adopt a categorical independent-judgment rule that could destabilize settled administrative regimes. On this record involving technical fisheries management under Magnuson–Stevens, a reasonable agency interpretation within a congressionally created gap remains appropriate for judicial review under § 706(2)(A).
